newsitem.title: UK: Crest shrugs off huge volume in market debutante.
newsitem.headline: Crest shrugs off huge volume in market debutante.

text.p: Crest, the electronic system which settles share trades in London, on Monday shrugged off the huge volume of trades in Alliance & Leicester Plc, one of its biggest tests since Crest started operations last July.

The real test, said head of public affairs Paul Symons, would come next week, when Alliance bargains done today would be matched under the London Stock Exchange's five-day "rolling settlement" regime.
"Today is a non-event as far as settlement is concerned," Symons said.
He said Crest remained confident that its recently-extended opening hours would enable it to cope with the increased volume generated by the flotation of the former building society -- and
"We are pretty confident but not at all complacent," Symons said.

Trading volume in Alliance reached 82.9 million shares by 1324 GMT, making it the most active stock in the London market by a wide margin. The stock was quoted at 561-1/2p, well ahead of market expectations.
Crest has brought forward its opening time to 1300 GMT on Monday morning to give brokers more time to input share deals, and is opening at 0430 GMT, the rest of the week.

Symons pointed out that today's volume would represent only a few thousand Crest transactions, since brokerage Cazenove was parcelling up shares sold pre-flotation by Alliance members, and placing them with investment institutions.

Crest, established in 1993 after the collapse of a London Stock Exchange attempt to replace share certificates with an electronic system, remains in the spotlight after its faltering early steps last year.
Bottlenecks in the system led to a backlog of share deals to be settled soon after its launch last July.
The system also slowed earlier this year as end of tax year deals clogged up the pipelines.

However, Crest earlier this month kept to its timetable to move settlement in all FTSE 100 stocks to the new paperless regime. It recently bolstered its computer capacity by 60 percent and enhanced its software to cope with ever-increasing calls on its service.
Bigger challenges lie ahead, when the biggest demutualisation, of Halifax building society, happens in June.
